5.title: Solutions, colloids, and suspensions differ in appearance and in how they treat light

members.title: Solutions, colloids, and suspensions differ in appearance and in how they treat light
members.content: The illustration shows three distinct types of mixtures. The first, labeled “Solution,” depicts a clear, uniform liquid where light passes straight through, and particles are too small to be seen or settle. The second, “Colloid,” shows a cloudy mixture where light is scattered inside, but the particles do not separate when the mixture is left undisturbed, like gatas, taho, or mayonesa. Finally, the third, “Suspension,” is a cloudy mixture with solid particles at the bottom that settle out over time, such as muddy water or gawgaw in water, and light is blocked.

members.title: Uniform and Non-Uniform Mixtures (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The Grade 6 competency asks learners to sort mixtures by appearance.
The question is simple: does A uniform mixture, also called a homogeneous mixture, looks the same in every part.
The components are so evenly spread that you cannot tell them apart by looking.

members.title: Uniform and Non-Uniform Mixtures (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
A glass of sugar water, a cup of brewed coffee without grounds, and a sip of buko juice all look like a single liquid, even though each one contains several materials.
Uniform mixtures of this kind are called solutions.
A non-uniform mixture, also called a heterogeneous mixture, shows its components.

members.title: Uniform and Non-Uniform Mixtures (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
You can see the separate parts, and different spoonfuls may not look the same.
A bowl of halo-halo, a plate of pancit, a handful of rice mixed with corn, and a glass of muddy water are all non-uniform.

members.title: Solutions: Solute and Solvent
members.content:
In a solution, the material that dissolves is the solute, and the material that does the dissolving is the solvent. In sweetened coffee, the sugar is the solute and the hot water is the solvent. The solvent is usually the component present in the greater amount, and water is so common as a solvent that it is often called the universal solvent.
Three conditions affect how quickly a solute dissolves, and learners can test each one:
Size of the particles. Finely ground sugar dissolves faster than a large lump, because more of its surface touches the water.
Stirring. A stirred glass dissolves its sugar faster than one left standing, because stirring keeps bringing fresh water into contact with the solute.
Temperature. Sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water, which is why powdered drinks mix easily in warm water but leave grains at the bottom of a cold glass.
Not every solute dissolves in every solvent. Salt and sugar dissolve in water, but cooking oil does not.
Oil and water separate into two layers no matter how long they are stirred, which is why a bottle of salad dressing must be shaken before use.

members.title: Suspensions and Colloids (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
Between the clear solution and the obviously separated mixture are two kinds worth naming.
A suspension is a non-uniform mixture in which solid particles are large enough to be seen and heavy enough to settle when the mixture is left alone.

members.title: Suspensions and Colloids (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Gawgaw stirred into water, muddy water from a flooded street, and a bottle of medicine labelled "shake well before using" are all suspensions.
Their particles can be trapped by filter paper.
A colloid sits in between.

members.title: Suspensions and Colloids (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Its particles are too small to settle out, so the mixture stays evenly cloudy for a long time, but they are still large enough to scatter light.
Gatas, taho, mayonesa, gulaman, and the smoke from burning leaves are colloids.
Shining a flashlight through a glass of milk reveals the beam

members.title: Air as a Mixture (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
Not all mixtures are liquids.
Air is a mixture of gases, and the Grade 6 competency names its main components: nitrogen, which makes up the largest share; oxygen, which living things need for respiration; carbon dioxide, which plants use to make food; and water vapor, whose amount rises and falls with the weather.

members.title: Air as a Mixture (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
Air is a uniform mixture: it looks the same throughout, and its gases do not settle into layers.
Because the components are only physically combined, each keeps its own properties — which is why oxygen can still support burning even while it is mixed with the other gases.

7.title: Changes in solid materials when bent, pressed, hammered, and cut

members.title: Changes in solid materials when bent, pressed, hammered, and cut
members.content: The image shows four distinct ways a solid material can be altered. The first illustration depicts a shape changing when a material is bent, but the size remains the same. The second shows a material being pressed, resulting in a flattened shape and the original amount of material remaining unchanged. The third illustrates a material being hammered, where the shape and thickness change, and the metal itself remains solid. Finally, the fourth shows a material being cut, resulting in multiple pieces, each retaining the same original material.

7.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 1 of 3)

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The Grade 5 competency moves from force to two conditions that cause deeper changes: application of heat and the presence or lack of oxygen.
Heat can cause a material to melt, evaporate, soften, harden, or burn.
Ice left on a saucer melts into water.

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Candle wax melts and then hardens again when it cools.
Sugar heated in a pan turns brown and gives off a sweet smell as it becomes caramel — and that change cannot be undone.
Oxygen is part of the air around us, and many changes depend on whether it is present.

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Iron exposed to air and moisture forms a reddish-brown coating called rust, which is why a bakal na pako left outdoors during the rainy season looks nothing like a new one.
A candle covered by a glass jar goes out because the oxygen inside is used up.
Sliced saging or mansanas turns brown when left on the table because its exposed flesh reacts with the oxygen in the air.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
By Grade 6, learners sort changes into two kinds.
A physical change alters only the appearance of a material — its size, shape, or state — while the material itself stays the same.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Physical changes are usually reversible: melted ice can be frozen again, a crumpled paper can be flattened, and dissolved salt can be recovered by evaporating the water.
A chemical change produces an entirely new material with new properties.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Chemical changes are irreversible: rust cannot be turned back into shiny iron, burnt wood cannot be turned back into wood, and a cooked egg cannot be uncooked.
Useful clues that a chemical change has taken place are a new color, a new smell, bubbles of gas, heat given off, or a solid forming where there was none.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The last Grade 4 competency asks learners to judge a change, not just describe it.
Many changes are useful.
Cutting cloth produces clothing.
Hammering metal produces tools.
Cooking makes food safe and easier to digest.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Decaying leaves in a compost pit become fertilizer for a school garden.
Other changes are harmful, especially to the environment.
Rust weakens roofing sheets and bridges.
Spoiled food causes illness.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Burning plastic and other household waste releases smoke and toxic gases into the air, which is why the practice is discouraged and is covered by the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act.
Learning to tell useful changes from harmful ones is what turns this lesson from a list of observations into a habit of responsible decision-making.
